exam: A patient with recent Campylobacter infection develops ascending weakness – what is the next urgent step? — Assess respiratory function (vital capacity) and start IV immunoglobulin or plasma exchange.

Explain why a demyelinating neuropathy shows prolonged distal latency but relatively preserved amplitude on NCS. — Nodes are damaged, slowing initiation; axons remain intact, so amplitude stays normal.
How does myelin loss alter the safety factor of conduction? — Reduces insulation, increasing leak; fewer Na⁺ channels at nodes lower the depolarising current, risking failure.
In a low‑resource setting without NCS, which bedside findings support a demyelinating process? — Symmetric, rapidly progressive weakness, areflexia, and preserved sensation early on.
Why is high‑dose steroids not first‑line for Guillain‑Barré? — Steroids have not shown benefit and may increase infection risk; IVIG or plasma exchange are evidence‑based.

A child with sickle cell disease presents with painful limb swelling – how could impaired saltatory conduction contribute? — Vaso‑occlusive infarction of peripheral nerves can cause demyelination, slowing conduction and producing neuropathic pain.

Differentiate between axonal and demyelinating neuropathy on clinical grounds. — Axonal: distal wasting, sensory loss dominates; Demyelinating: rapid weakness, prominent reflex loss, sensory relatively spared.

What laboratory result would mislead you in diagnosing Guillain‑Barré in a malaria‑endemic area? — Elevated CSF white cells from concurrent malaria meningitis could be misinterpreted as infection rather than pure demyelination.
ai.title: Saltatory Conduction in Myelinated Nerves
ai.subject: Physiology
ai.summary: Saltatory conduction is the rapid propagation of action potentials along myelinated axons via nodes of Ranvier. It underlies fast nerve signaling and is impaired in demyelinating diseases common in low‑resource settings.

b: Velocity up to 120 m/s vs 1 m/s in unmyelinated fibers
sections.p: In myelinated peripheral and central nerves, the myelin sheath insulates the axon, leaving periodic gaps called nodes of Ranvier. Action potentials ‘jump’ from node to node, greatly increasing conduction velocity.

b: Myelin produced by Schwann cells (PNS) or oligodendrocytes (CNS)
Node length ≈ 1 µm; internode length 0.5–2 mm
Conduction speed proportional to internode length and myelin thickness
sections.p: The insulating myelin forces depolarisation to occur only at nodes where voltage‑gated Na⁺ channels are concentrated. This creates a regenerative, stepwise propagation.

b: Peripheral neuropathy in HIV, TB meningitis, malaria‑related neuropathy
Multiple sclerosis (central demyelination) – less common locally but important
sections.p: Loss of myelin disrupts saltatory conduction, leading to slowed or blocked nerve signals. Recognising the pattern helps diagnose demyelinating disorders and guides urgent management.

t.b: Is conduction velocity reduced? → Confirms demyelination; if unavailable, rely on clinical pattern and CSF analysis
Elevated protein with normal cell count? → Supports Guillain‑Barré; if lumbar puncture not feasible, use bedside reflex testing

b: Explain why myelin increases speed (reduces capacitance, increases resistance)
Describe how node density of Na⁺ channels enables regeneration
Link clinical signs (areflexia, weakness) to disrupted saltatory conduction
sections.p: Examiners test understanding of physiology, interpretation of slowed conduction, and management of acute demyelination.

b: Do not assume diabetic neuropathy is demyelinating; it is primarily axonal
Avoid equating peripheral and central myelin – different glial cells
sections.p: Students often confuse slowed conduction with axonal loss or attribute all neuropathies to metabolic causes.

whenToSeekHelp: Rapidly progressing weakness, respiratory compromise, or autonomic instability in a patient with suspected Guillain‑Barré
